text: Every technique in this course — port scanning, exploitation, password attacks — is also, word for word, a description of a crime. In the United States, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act makes unauthorized access to a protected computer a federal offense, with no exception for good intentions. The UK's Computer Misuse Act works the same way. So before anything else in this course, we need to talk about the one thing that turns these techniques into a lawful, paid engagement instead: a signature.

A Slack message saying 'go ahead and test our app' is not authorization. Real authorization is a signed contract plus a Rules of Engagement document, agreed to by someone who actually has legal authority over the systems — a system owner or named executive sponsor, not just whichever employee happens to be your point of contact. And if the application runs on a third party's infrastructure, your client's signature alone doesn't cover testing someone else's systems — that vendor needs to sign off too.

A professional Rules of Engagement document, consistent with how the Penetration Testing Execution Standard treats pre-engagement interactions, spells out the testing window with exact dates and any blackout periods, the in-scope systems by exact IP range or hostname, explicit out-of-scope exclusions, which techniques are permitted or prohibited, named emergency contacts reachable for the full engagement, and an escalation procedure for critical findings. Vague scope like 'the whole network' doesn't belong in a real ROE.

That escalation procedure earns its own line item because two things go wrong without one. First, a tester who finds an actively exploitable critical flaw — say, a server someone else has already compromised — needs to report it immediately, not bury it in a report delivered weeks later. Second, a client's own incident response team may detect the authorized test's traffic and treat it as a real attack. The emergency contact is who confirms, in real time, that it's the pentest they hired.

That's the foundation everything else in this course rests on: real authorization, from someone who actually has the authority to grant it, documented in a signed Rules of Engagement before any testing activity begins. Next lesson, we turn that authorization into a precise, written scope — defining exactly which systems are in bounds and which aren't, so neither the client nor the tester is ever surprised by what gets touched.
